title: Follow-up to my one-sentence AI trader: you can't backtest vibes, so I made it turn the sentence into actual rules
author: murdocc007
selftext:
A couple of weeks ago [I posted](https://www.reddit.com/r/ai_trading/comments/1w6tri3/i_gave_an_llm_agent_my_robinhood_account_for_3/) about letting an LLM trade from a one-sentence strategy. The problem I skipped over: the model re-reads your sentence on every run and decides from scratch. Same strategy, same market, and it can still make a different call. That also makes backtesting meaningless. "What would it have done in March?" has no stable answer if the model reinterprets you each time.

So I built it the other way round. You still describe the strategy in plain English, but the LLM is only involved while you're building it. It turns what you wrote into explicit rules, and then it's out of the loop. The rules run on a schedule, and the same inputs always give the same decision. Which means you can backtest before it touches the $100k paper account.

The flow is four screens (they're in the images): pick the agent type(flux)

https://preview.redd.it/e4ybaboyhyrh1.png?width=2236&format=png&auto=webp&s=a314caebc8b59b2af4762add88f4cb606f77dce0

pick a universe (S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, a sector, or your own tickers)

https://preview.redd.it/ctdzh472iyrh1.png?width=2682&format=png&auto=webp&s=0092218c89ed3a49062c36ce0fcb602d244eb2d9

  
  
describe the strategy

https://preview.redd.it/oc7c24c4iyrh1.png?width=2628&format=png&auto=webp&s=597cc1e96f04fc3e400e784284613dc4c2817aef

 backtest.

https://preview.redd.it/3we9d8s5iyrh1.png?width=2650&format=png&auto=webp&s=9b0777144bc1dc80238acba89e3a6205f3a31c79

Here's what I typed to test it: *"Buy S&P 500 stocks when their 14-day RSI drops below 30, sized at 5% of portfolio each, with an 8% take profit and a 5% stop loss. Check daily."*

And here's what it turned that into:

    universe: S&P 500
    signal:   rsi(14, daily) < 30
    action:   buy, 5% of portfolio per position
    exits:    5% stop, 8% take-profit
    checks:   daily

Seeing it written out is most of the value. Half the time what I type and what I mean aren't the same, and you only find out when the rule is in front of you.

The backtest over the last 6 months: **+2.25%, 424 closed trades, no slippage modelled.** So a textbook oversold-bounce strategy churned through hundreds of trades for a return that realistic trading costs would probably wipe out. I haven't compared it to just holding SPY over the same stretch, but I wouldn't bet on it winning. Which is kind of the point: I'd have happily run that live on vibes.

Here's a [live version](https://wallstreetclaws.com/agents/98deaa7f-38cf-40f8-9ae5-b89adb0db088) of a quant agent which is actually profitable.

  
Limitations, so nobody's surprised:

* It checks at most hourly and only during market hours.
* The price data lags a bit by design, so anything that depends on the first few minutes of a move won't work.
* Backtests are easy to fool yourself with. Tweak until the curve looks great and you've just fitted the past.
* Paper money only, and it's in beta.

What I'd actually like feedback on:

1. Is "LLM writes the rules once, then gets out of the way" a useful split, or is this just a rule-based backtester with a chat box on the front?
2. What would you need to see in a backtest before trusting it? I show trades, P&L and no slippage right now. A benchmark line, costs and out-of-sample splits are the obvious gaps.
3. What rules or indicators would you reach for first that you'd expect to be missing?

It's at [wallstreetclaws.com](http://wallstreetclaws.com) if you want to try building one. Not advice.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
The useful part of that split is making ambiguities visible before execution. Your \`rsi(14, daily) < 30\` rule still leaves a question: buy once when RSI crosses below 30, or buy on every daily check while it stays there? With 5% per position, repeated signals also need an explicit rule for adding to existing holdings.

I'd test a tiny example where one stock stays below 30 for three days, then another where 25 S&P 500 stocks qualify together. Show the expected orders, including how available cash determines which qualify for purchase. Those choices could materially change the 424 closed trades. The screenshots aren't available here, so I'd check whether the generated rules expose those choices for confirmation. That would make the chat interface useful beyond translating indicator names.

replies.author: CHSJournal
replies.body:
As far as I understand it works at a portfolio level, so every decision is go long, go short, hold or exit.  
I personally prefer this approach but I can imagine with higher frequencies I rather have agent make a trade decision rather than a portfolio decision.  
I am always weighing pros and cons of both approaches - do you think one is better than the other?

comments.author: FaithlessnessFit2900
comments.body: It's cool that you can backtest these strategies.. because modifying the strategy requires me to make an llm call, it takes a few seconds. Can you add a feature so I can directly edit the strategy instead of going through the LLM chat?

replies.author: QT_WSC
replies.body: How do you imagine that to be? Directly modifying the text in nodes of graph?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
compiling once is the right call, it fixes the reproducibility problem. the one it opens is that the compile step knows the future: a model turning "buy the dip" into thresholds today has read every dip through last month, so the rules it picks are quietly fitted to the same window you then backtest on. what worked for me is freezing the compiled rules and grading them on a stretch nobody chose, the most recent few months, since neither you nor the model have opinions about those yet.

this is also how I built Quantradin: the model only drafts the rules, a separate engine runs the backtest and the paper desk, and the model never sees a fill. free, paper only, and the name matches my handle here. would genuinely like to compare notes on the compile step.

replies.author: murdocc007
replies.body: Sounds good. Dm on how you want exchange notes.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: works for me, though I'd keep the meat of it here since the compile step is the bit most people in this sub get wrong. first thing I'd want to see is how you freeze the rules once they're compiled.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body:
1. It's a real distinction, not just cosmetic — the value isn't the parsing step, it's that a fixed rule set makes the strategy falsifiable. "LLM re-reads and reinterprets every run" means you're testing the model's mood, not the strategy; freezing it into `rsi(14) < 30` means you're testing the strategy. That's the whole point of a backtest existing at all.
2. Benchmark line and costs are the two that actually change the verdict here — +2.25% over 6 months with 424 trades and no slippage almost certainly loses to holding SPY once you model even conservative costs (bid-ask + a few bps slippage per leg, times 424 round trips adds up fast). Out-of-sample split matters less for something this simple (RSI(14)<30 isn't expressive enough to overfit hard), but costs alone probably flip this from "works" to "doesn't."
3. First things I'd expect missing: a volatility or regime filter (RSI oversold in a strong downtrend just means "still falling," not "bounce coming"), and volume/liquidity confirmation so you're not sizing 5% into something that gaps past your stop before it fills.

One thing worth flagging on the data side since you mentioned the price lag is by design: that's exactly where a lot of these "profitable in backtest" systems quietly fall apart live, since a rule that looks clean on lagged daily bars can behave very differently once real-time event timing (earnings, halts, news prints) is what's actually moving the name intraday — which is the layer EventTrader's data pipeline is built to handle more precisely than a generic delayed feed.

comments.author: CODE_HEIST
comments.body: the split is useful, but the generated rule should become a versioned spec rather than just readable text. i’d add a diff and confirmation step, then tests for repeated signals, simultaneous candidates, cash limits, missing data and stop/target conflicts. benchmark, costs and untouched data matter, but so does reproducing the exact same orders after reloading the saved rule.
